fatal_errors: The intervention does not reconstruct the target study, which examined CrFeTaVW-to-CrFeTiVW substitution, hybrid MD/Monte Carlo simulations, mechanical alloying, SPS consolidation, segregation, and thermal diffusivity rather than Y-modified TiVNbTa.
Adding elemental Y alone does not ensure formation of a controlled Y2O3 dispersion; no oxygen source, oxygen activity, oxidation route, or oxide volume fraction is specified.

The cited evidence does not demonstrate Y2O3 dispersion strengthening in TiVNbTa at 1273 K. E2 concerns TiO-containing NbMoTaWVTi and mainly reports room-temperature strength, while E1 contains no Y or oxide-dispersion intervention.

The proposed experiment does not test thermal conductivity or diffusivity, W/alloy and alloy/CuCrZr interface stability, thermal-expansion mismatch, or thermal-cycle-induced damage, all of which are central to the intended heat-transfer-layer application.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the stated elevated-temperature strength loss and proposes a scientifically recognizable oxide-dispersion-strengthening mechanism. Its matched control, high-temperature mechanical testing, TEM, and EBSD could discriminate whether a produced dispersion correlates with improved strength. However, it is not a reconstruction of the hidden target in composition, intervention, mechanism, conditions, measurements, or outcomes. More importantly, the proposed single intervention—minor Y addition—does not by itself establish that Y2O3 nanoparticles will form. The supporting papers only establish general high-temperature behavior or precipitation strengthening in related refractory alloys, not this specific chemistry and temperature. Boundary conditions are also incomplete: strain rate, loading mode, dwell time, atmosphere, thermal-cycle profile, interfacial geometry, and heat-transfer performance are unspecified. The idea is therefore plausible in general but insufficiently supported as formulated.
